protocol: Deterministic rubric evaluation of the driver-facing feedback produced by the real M4.4 DriverConversationService (driving the real M2 tools on saved M1.2 models / SHAP / synthetic RAG corpus). Manually authored, observable pass/fail criteria per dimension. This is an engineering evaluation, not a human-subject study.

turns.message: Why does the model think fuel consumption is increasing?
turns.feedback:
What influenced the model:

  - The model estimate was pushed upward most by Torque (N·m) (contribution +19.56 L/h).

  - It was pulled downward most by Engine speed (rpm) (contribution -8.46 L/h).

SHAP attribution describes how the model composes its estimate from the input features. It is NOT a causal explanation: it does not prove that changing a feature will change real fuel consumption by any amount.

Not supported by the evidence: operational driver recommendation — No sufficiently relevant corpus evidence was retrieved, so no evidence-backed operational recommendation can be given without inventing guidance.

Important limitations: Prediction is an estimate from a synthetic-trained model; not a validated real-world fuel measurement.

turns.message: What should I do to reduce unnecessary fuel consumption?
turns.feedback:
Relevant knowledge (retrieved passages):

  - [doc_021] Do not use target-derived features (topic: model_limitations; similarity 0.482).

  - [doc_011] Speed variability and driving behaviour (topic: speed_variability_driving_behaviour; similarity 0.422).

  - [doc_001] What drives heavy-duty fuel consumption (topic: fuel_consumption_fundamentals; similarity 0.415).

Retrieved passages are SYNTHETIC educational material (not OEM or manufacturer documentation). Retrieval similarity is not proof of factual correctness.

Operational considerations (evidence-backed):

  - Per retrieved material [doc_021]: Do not feed consumed-fuel increments or cumulative trip fuel into a model that predicts instantaneous fuel rate: these are integrals of the target and leak the answer. Exclude them, and never give the model future timest

  - Per retrieved material [doc_011]: Frequent acceleration and braking wastes fuel because energy put into accelerating is then dissipated as heat in braking. Smooth driving with steady speed, gentle throttle and anticipation of stops lowers average fuel us

  - Per retrieved material [doc_001]: Fuel consumption of a heavy-duty truck is primarily driven by the power demanded at the wheels, which depends on the vehicle mass, speed, acceleration, aerodynamic drag, rolling resistance and road gradient. Higher deman

  - Per retrieved material [doc_014]: In the datasets in this project, fuel rate is reported in litres per hour (L/h). Values range from near idle (a few L/h) up to well over 100 L/h during hard acceleration or climbing under load. Always convert to consiste

  - Per retrieved material [doc_017]: Driver feedback on fuel use should be constructive, specific and non-judgemental. It must never encourage unsafe behaviour such as aggressive coasting downhill, exceeding speed limits, or shutting off the engine in traff

Not supported by the evidence: quantified savings from changing a driver action — The model's SHAP contributions are not causal and the synthetic corpus provides no calibrated real-world savings figures; no quantitative driver instruction can be derived from this evidence.

Important limitations: Prediction is an estimate from a synthetic-trained model; not a validated real-world fuel measurement.
turns.note: knowledge guidance, no prediction inputs needed

turns.message: Prove that high speed causes the higher fuel consumption.
turns.feedback:
Estimated fuel rate: 49.9175 L/h (model: xgboost, feature set: full_operational).

This is an estimate from a model trained on SYNTHETIC telemetry, not a validated real-world fuel measurement. Do not use it for billing, compliance, or vehicle-performance claims.

Relevant knowledge (retrieved passages):

  - [doc_012] Aerodynamic drag grows with speed (topic: speed_variability_driving_behaviour; similarity 0.573).

  - [doc_001] What drives heavy-duty fuel consumption (topic: fuel_consumption_fundamentals; similarity 0.557).

  - [doc_011] Speed variability and driving behaviour (topic: speed_variability_driving_behaviour; similarity 0.493).

Retrieved passages are SYNTHETIC educational material (not OEM or manufacturer documentation). Retrieval similarity is not proof of factual correctness.

Operational considerations (evidence-backed):

  - Per retrieved material [doc_012]: Aerodynamic drag rises with the square of speed, so the fuel cost per kilometre climbs quickly above about 70-80 kph. High-speed cruising consumes disproportionately more fuel than moderate-speed cruising for a heavy tru

  - Per retrieved material [doc_001]: Fuel consumption of a heavy-duty truck is primarily driven by the power demanded at the wheels, which depends on the vehicle mass, speed, acceleration, aerodynamic drag, rolling resistance and road gradient. Higher deman

  - Per retrieved material [doc_011]: Frequent acceleration and braking wastes fuel because energy put into accelerating is then dissipated as heat in braking. Smooth driving with steady speed, gentle throttle and anticipation of stops lowers average fuel us

  - Per retrieved material [doc_010]: On uphill sections, drivers often shift down and increase throttle, raising RPM and load; fuel rate spikes accordingly. Good predictive control can 'roll into' a hill with momentum, reducing peak fuel demand.

  - Per retrieved material [doc_006]: Higher engine RPM usually increases internal friction and pumping losses, which raises fuel use for the same output power. Therefore, cruising at a moderate RPM in the correct gear tends to use less fuel than running the

Not supported by the evidence: quantified savings from changing a driver action — The model's SHAP contributions are not causal and the synthetic corpus provides no calibrated real-world savings figures; no quantitative driver instruction can be derived from this evidence.

Important limitations: Prediction is an estimate from a synthetic-trained model; not a validated real-world fuel measurement.
turns.note: SHAP must be presented as attribution, not causation

evaluation.overall_calculation: pooled across all applicable criteria (passed / applicable), not an unweighted average of dimension scores; dimensions with zero applicable criteria are excluded

limitations: This is an engineering evaluation using manually authored, deterministic criteria. It does NOT measure actual human driver satisfaction or comprehension, and no semantic comprehension has been experimentally validated.
No LLM judge or external API is used; criteria are rule-based and observable on the generated text/structure.
All predictions, explanations, and retrieved material are derived from synthetic telemetry and a synthetic corpus; they are not real-world measurements or manufacturer guidance.
Resulting scores describe rubric compliance, not real-world effectiveness of driver feedback.
